title: Aquinas: it all seems like straw
hookLine: after an experience at Mass he stopped writing, saying all his work seemed like straw

lines: A GREAT WORK, QUESTION BY QUESTION.
cards: Straw. That's the word he used. The quiet student has grown into a great teacher.

For years he has been writing a vast work explaining the Christian faith, question by question, dictating to helpers. Then one morning in Naples he says Mass, and something happens. The sources never say what.
Afterward he puts down his pen. He won't write or dictate. His friend and companion, Reginald, begs him to go on, and Thomas gives a strange answer.

teach.h: STRAW, COMPARED WITH WHAT I HAVE SEEN.
teach.b: The account comes from testimony gathered after his death, when the church was looking into his life. Reginald presses him: why stop now? And Thomas says, in effect: I can't.
Everything I have written seems like straw to me, compared with what I have seen. That's the whole story. He never says what he saw, or explains it, or teaches it.
The great work, the one people still call the Summa, is left unfinished, and he dies not long after, on a journey. What do you do with that? First, notice what he didn't say.
He didn't say his work was false, or burn it. Straw isn't poison.
Straw is what grain grows on; it holds the wheat up, and then the harvest is gathered and the straw left in the field. The church kept reading him, and still does.
Second, notice where it happened: at Mass, in prayer, not at a desk. Thomas spent his life using reason to speak about God, and believed reason was a gift.
But Paul had already said our knowing has a limit: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face." Some readers hear in the straw a man who glimpsed the face.
Some wonder whether he was ill or worn out, and say both could be true. The sources don't settle it. They leave a teacher who stopped talking, and a silence where the rest of his book should be.

how: Catholic students and teachers still study the Summa Theologiae, and the story of the straw is told in retreats and sermons about the limits of words before God.

o: the teacher who called his great work straw
the pope who settled the debates of his day
a monk who burned his books as worthless

p: Paul on the limit of knowing

s: Thomas said his writings were false and should be burned
he said they seemed like straw compared with what he had seen. he never called them false.
Thomas explained what he saw at Mass
he never said what he saw. the sources leave it unexplained.
after that morning, the great work was left unfinished
he stopped writing and dictating, and the Summa was never completed.

games.q: you're Reginald. your friend Thomas has stopped writing his great work and won't say why. what do you do?
o: finish it for him without asking.
press him to go on, and ask why he stopped.
leave quietly and tell no one.
games.why: Reginald begs him to go on. Thomas answers that all he has written seems like straw compared with what he has seen.

practice: Put down whatever you're holding, the phone, the pen, the plan for the next hour, and for this minute add no words of your own, letting each thought go by like a cart on a far road.
If you pray, you can sit with a line from the prophet Habakkuk, let all the earth keep silence before him; if not, let the quiet be full.

wordCard.voice: Aquinas. Thomas Aquinas, the teacher who explained the faith question by question, and then stopped writing, saying it all seemed like straw beside what he had seen.

carryVoice: Your line: all is straw. Straw isn't poison; it holds the wheat up. Until tomorrow.
